theme: Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior
title: The Second Channel
tagline: Empathy at work: hearing what isn't said.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for all Vanderbilt staff: notice the tone and energy shifts colleagues actually communicate with, check in instead of assuming, and answer the feeling in a message before its content.
heroLead: Colleagues rarely say the important thing straight out. It arrives as a flat 'fine', a camera that stays off, a joke with an edge. This session trains your ear for those shifts, and the small check-in that answers them.
objectives: Notice tone and energy shifts that carry more information than the words
Check in with a light, open question instead of assuming what a shift means
Answer the feeling in a message before answering its content
missionTie: A century-defining university is built on thousands of working relationships, and empathy is what keeps them working. Hearing colleagues well is everyday culture work, the human layer of Exceptional Core Operations.
goalLead: The manager standard runs on coaching, and coaching runs on listening. This session builds the listening for everyone, because every colleague shapes how heard people feel at work.

agenda.d: Tone, pace, and energy carry the message the words leave out.
What a light, open check-in sounds like, and why guessing goes wrong.
Answering the frustration first is what makes the facts land.

manifesto: People tell you how they are before they tell you what they think. Listen in that order.

sections.headline: The message rides the tone.
sections.lead: Every conversation runs on two channels: the words, and everything around them. When a chatty teammate answers in one line, or a steady voice speeds up, the second channel is broadcasting. The skill starts with noticing the change from that person's normal.
sections.group: In pairs: what is one 'tell' you have learned to read in a colleague, a shift in tone, pace, or energy? Roles, never names.
sections.solo: Name one 'tell' you have learned to read in a colleague: a shift in tone, pace, or energy. Roles, never names.

card.text: Shifts only mean something against a baseline. Quiet is no signal from a quiet person; it is a loud one from a talker. Read the change from this person's normal, and hold your first guess about what it means loosely.

interaction.q: A teammate who usually fills the room writes 'fine, whatever works' about a plan they built. What matters most here?

opts.t: The words: they agreed, so the plan proceeds
opts.why: The words say yes; the shift says something else. Proceeding on the words alone spends trust you may want later.

opts.t: The shift from their normal: that is the message
opts.why: Right. From this person, flatness is loud. You do not yet know what it means, and that is exactly what a check-in is for.

opts.t: Nothing; moods are private and work is work
opts.why: Their inner life is theirs, and the working signal still touches the work. Noticing a shift is attention, and it costs one small check-in.

sections.headline: Ask the shift, lightly.
sections.lead: A noticed shift is a hypothesis. Guessing turns it into a verdict ('you're clearly upset') and ignoring lets it harden on its own. The move in between is a light, private, open check-in that lets the person tell you what is true, including 'all good'.
sections.group: In pairs: say a check-in line out loud that you could actually use tomorrow. Trade lines and keep the better one.
sections.solo: Write one check-in line you could actually use tomorrow, in your own voice.

interaction.intro: You noticed a shift. Read what happens next and call the move.
interaction.passMsg: You have the move. Notice the shift, keep your guess loose, and offer an easy open door in private.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: a real check-in is private, easy to decline, and open about what the shift means. Guesses tell; check-ins ask.

items.q: A colleague goes quiet in a planning call. Afterward you message: 'You seemed annoyed we cut your item. You okay?'
items.why: Private and kind, and still a guess. Naming their feeling for them means they now have to manage your theory. Try: 'You went quiet back there. Anything you'd add?'

items.q: A teammate's messages have been short and flat for a week. You figure it will pass, and say nothing.
items.why: Maybe it passes; meanwhile they spent the week reading your silence too. A week-long shift has earned thirty seconds of 'how are you doing, actually?'

items.q: After a tense meeting you message privately: 'That got heated. How are you landing? No need to answer.'
items.why: Private, open, and easy to decline. It answers the shift without naming feelings for them, and the exit ramp makes honesty cheaper.

sections.headline: Answer the feeling, then the facts.
sections.lead: When a message arrives carrying frustration, most of us answer the content and skip the feeling, and the sender hears half a reply. Answering the feeling takes one plain sentence, and it is the sentence that makes the rest of your answer land as help.

interaction.intro: A colleague writes: 'The data STILL isn't ready. I've asked three times and my report is due Friday. Whatever, I'll figure it out.' Build your reply.

opts.t: 'The data pipeline runs Wednesdays, so it should be there tomorrow.'
opts.coach: Accurate and deaf. The frustration went unanswered, so the facts arrive sounding like a shrug.

opts.t: 'Sorry for the delay! Let me look into it right away.'
opts.coach: Polite and quick, and it skips what they actually said: three asks, a deadline, and giving up. Speed reads as brush-off when the feeling goes unnamed.

opts.t: 'Three asks with Friday looming? That's genuinely frustrating.'
opts.coach: The feeling, answered plainly and first. One sentence of being heard changes how every fact after it sounds.

opts.t: 'For what it's worth, my part was done on time.'
opts.coach: A defense they did not ask for. Now the thread is about fault, and Friday is still coming.

opts.t: 'I'll chase the data team and get back to you.'
opts.coach: Helpful and vague. Without a time attached, 'I'll get back to you' is one more thing for them to chase.

opts.t: 'I'm on it now. You'll have the data or a workaround by 3pm today.'
opts.coach: Concrete relief with a clock on it. The 'whatever, I'll figure it out' just stopped being true.

heads.strong: A whole reply. They felt heard in the first line and helped by the second, and the edge went out of the thread.
heads.mid: A half reply. Useful content over an unanswered feeling; workable, and the frustration is still looking for a door.
heads.weak: A miss. The facts were fine, the person felt managed, and Friday's report now comes with a grudge attached.

reactions.strong: They write back 'thank you, seriously.' Next time something slips they come to you early and calm, because being heard once made asking feel safe.
reactions.mid: The data arrives, the report ships, and the colleague quietly starts copying your manager on requests. Content without acknowledgment taught them to escalate.
reactions.weak: Friday's report ships late with a pointed footnote about data availability. The relationship now runs on receipts.

recap.q: A normally lively colleague gives one-word answers all morning. The signal is...
opts: The shift from their normal baseline
Proof that something is badly wrong
recap.why: Shifts read against a baseline. You know something changed; you do not yet know what, and that is what a check-in is for.

recap.q: The best response to a noticed shift is...
opts: Name the feeling you think they have
Wait for them to bring it up
Ask a mutual colleague what is up
recap.why: Open and easy to decline beats a confident guess, and asking a third party turns a check-in into gossip.

recap.q: A frustrated message deserves a reply that starts with...
opts: One plain sentence answering the feeling
A defense of your own part in it
Forwarding it to the right team
recap.why: Feeling first, then content. Being heard is what makes the facts land as help instead of a shrug.

recapMsgs.high: The ear is tuned. Now point it at one real shift you have noticed.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the section you missed, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One shift you noticed. One check-in.
capstone.lead: Think of a colleague whose second channel has changed lately. Role only, never a name; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Whose shift have you noticed? Role and the change.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. project teammate; camera off and one-line answers for two weeks

practices.name: The quiet check-in
practices.move: Privately and lightly: 'I noticed you've been quieter lately. How are you doing, actually? No need to answer.'

practices.name: The feeling-first reply
practices.move: Next charged message you get, answer the feeling in your first sentence and the content in your second.

practices.name: The baseline read
practices.move: For one week, learn one colleague's normal: tone, pace, energy. Baselines are what make shifts readable.

whens.out: The check-in happens today, while the shift is fresh and the door is easy to open.
The check-in happens this week, in private, at a moment with no audience.
The next frustrated message you receive gets the feeling-first treatment before anything else.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did you learn that the words alone never told you?

closing.headline: Heard people hear better.
closing.lead: You built a baseline ear, a light check-in, and a feeling-first reply. That listening is the ground floor of this month's coaching theme, whichever side of a coaching conversation you sit on.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Make the check-in on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it as built: private, light, easy to decline. Then watch what the second channel does next; being heard changes it.

facilitator.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no one is assumed to manage people. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; this session closes the week in February's Coaching as the Core Manager Behavior month.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the check-in on your card happen? What did you learn that the words never said? Whose baseline are you learning now?' Share-backs feed the month's story bank for the coaching theme.

s1.title: The second channel
s1.purpose: Teach shift-noticing against a personal baseline: tone, pace, and energy over words.
s1.say: Think about the last time a colleague said 'fine' and you knew it was anything but. You were reading the second channel: tone, pace, energy, everything around the words. Everyone broadcasts on it, and most of us only listen when it gets loud. The skill starts smaller than that: knowing a person's normal well enough to notice when it changes.
facilitate: Read the baseline rule from the card; it reframes quiet colleagues immediately.
Run the knowledge check; everyone answers on their own screen.
Run the breakout on the 'tell' they have learned to read, roles only.

ask.q: Whose baseline do you know best, and what is their tell?
expect: A realization that they only know a few baselines
ask.respond: Both are useful. Baselines come free with attention, so you already own several. The gap is usually the colleagues you only ever meet in meetings.

s1.debrief: Shifts read against a baseline, and a shift is a hypothesis, never a verdict.
s1.watchFor: Diagnosis creep: 'quiet means disengaged.' Pull it back every time. Noticing is the skill; the meaning belongs to the person.
s1.transition: You noticed the shift. The next move decides whether noticing helps.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; collect two 'tells' in chat and move on.

s2.title: The check-in
s2.purpose: Replace assuming and ignoring with the light, private, open check-in.
s2.say: A noticed shift puts three moves on the table. You can assume, which is a guess wearing certainty. You can ignore, which the person reads as an answer anyway. Or you can check in: private, light, open, easy to decline. 'You went quiet back there, anything you'd add?' costs thirty seconds, and it is the difference between guessing at people and asking them.
facilitate: Run Assume, ignore, or check in? live on everyone's screens.
After round one, linger: the guess was private and kind and still a guess.
Run the breakout: say a check-in line aloud in your own voice.

ask.q: What makes 'no need to answer' such a strong ending for a check-in?
expect: It removes the pressure to perform an answer
It proves the door is real
ask.respond: Right. An exit ramp makes honesty cheaper. Half the value of a check-in lands even when the answer is 'all good.'

s2.debrief: Private, light, open, easy to decline. The check-in hands the meaning back to the person instead of guessing it for them.
s2.watchFor: Scripted-sounding lines in the breakout. Push for their own voice; a borrowed phrase reads as a technique, and techniques get polite answers.
s2.transition: Check-ins cover the shifts you see. The last section covers the feelings that arrive in writing.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one line from chat.

s3.title: Feeling before content
s3.purpose: Train the feeling-first reply: one plain sentence answering the emotion before any facts or fixes.
s3.say: Sometimes the second channel arrives in writing: capital letters in the middle of a message and a 'whatever, I'll figure it out' at the end. The reflex is to answer the content, because the content has an answer. A frustrated message is two messages, though, and if you only answer the facts, the person heard you ignore the other one. One plain sentence for the feeling first. Then the facts land as help.
facilitate: Run Answer the whole message; two minutes for both lines, then send it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: name the frustration plainly, then relief with a clock on it.

ask.q: Why does the quick apology in slot one still land badly?
expect: It is generic; it could answer any message
It skips what they actually said
Speed without acknowledgment reads as brush-off
ask.respond: Yes. The apology answers that a message arrived; the strong line answers what the message carried. People can tell which one they got.

s3.debrief: Feeling first, one plain sentence, then concrete help with a time attached. That order is the whole skill.
s3.watchFor: Overwrought feeling-lines that sound like a script. One plain sentence beats a paragraph of validation; this is workplace listening, kept light.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you pick your person and build the check-in card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One colleague whose second channel has shifted, role only, never a name. Pick the move, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it this week. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: That closes the coaching week. Monday gave managers the coaching moment, Tuesday put growth on the record for everyone, and today built the listening underneath both. Run the check-in on your card, and bring what the second channel taught you into next week's sessions. If you want to keep pulling the thread, Sara Canaday's Coaching Skills for Leaders and Managers is this month's LinkedIn Learning pick, and the navigator-led GROW practicum is a friendly place to practice this kind of listening out loud. Same rhythm next week; a new month and a new goal arrive in March.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone shares a heavy personal situation live on the call
contingencies.then: Receive it with one warm sentence, then protect them from the group: 'Thank you for trusting us with that; let's talk after.' Follow up privately and point to support resources where it fits.

contingencies.if: Someone objects that reading tone is mind-reading or overstepping
contingencies.then: Agree with the caution: the skill is noticing a change and asking, never diagnosing. The check-in hands the meaning back to the person, which is the opposite of mind-reading.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't this asking me to be my colleagues' therapist?
toughQuestions.a: No. The move is a thirty-second check-in and one feeling-first sentence, both ordinary collegial behavior. Anything heavier gets a warm handoff toward real support, and knowing that limit is part of the skill. You are a colleague who listens well; that is the whole job.

toughQuestions.q: What if I check in and I'm wrong, and it gets awkward?
toughQuestions.a: A light, open check-in has a built-in exit: 'all good' ends it with no harm done. People remember being noticed kindly far longer than they remember a guess that missed. The awkwardness lives in naming feelings for people, which is exactly what the check-in avoids.

toughQuestions.q: What about tone in email and chat, where there is no voice?
toughQuestions.a: Baselines still work: message length, response speed, punctuation, the emoji that went missing. Read the change against that person's normal, the same rule as voice. Then move the check-in itself somewhere richer; a shift noticed in chat rarely untangles in chat.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Thursday, 45 minutes on hearing what isn't said. Bring the memory of one moment a colleague's tone told you more than their words. You will never be asked to name anyone. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the check-in happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the check-in on your card happen? 2) What did you learn that the words never said? 3) Whose baseline are you learning now?
